source: Atkinson, Derry, Renkl and Wortham (2000) Learning from examples: instructional principles from the worked examples research. Review of Educational Research 70(2)
finding: Defines a worked example as a problem statement plus an expert's step-by-step solution. Traces the paradigm to Sweller's schema-acquisition work (1982-85): practice-only problem solving, the norm then, was beaten by pairing problems with examples. Says Zhu and Simon (1987) ran the first and most cited classroom study.
numbers: Review, no pooled number. Cites Sweller and Cooper 1985, Cooper and Sweller 1987, Ward and Sweller 1990, Carroll 1994 as pro-example.
quote: The best way to teach children how to solve problems is to give them lots of problems to solve
limits: Narrative review written before the 2023 meta-analysis. Most cited studies are lab studies in maths, physics and programming.
agent_relevance: Frame for our subgoal library: store a solved problem as problem plus stepwise solution, and show it before asking the agent to search from scratch.

source: Atkinson et al. (2000), skill-acquisition section, using the ACT-R four-stage model of Anderson, Fincham and Douglass (1997)
finding: Skill acquisition has four overlapping stages: solve by analogy to known examples; build abstract declarative rules; smooth automatic performance; retrieve stored instances. Worked examples matter most in stage 1 and early stage 2. They are not the preferred route to stage 3 (automation), where practice is key.
numbers: Four stages; no experimental numbers in this passage.
limits: A framing, not a test. Experts can still study other experts' performance for style.
agent_relevance: A rule for when to show a stored example (first contact with a problem class) and when to stop (class is routine).

source: Tarmizi and Sweller (1988) experiments 3-5, as summarised by Atkinson et al. (2000): split attention in geometry examples
finding: A worked-example advantage is not automatic. When diagram and text had to be mentally combined (split source), worked examples gave no advantage and conventional problems were faster on posttest time. Integrating the text into the diagram restored the advantage.
numbers: Exp 3: six pairs of circle-geometry problems, first of each pair worked. No significant difference on any measure; conventional faster on posttest time. Exps 4-5: integrated format beat conventional and split-source.
quote: guidance provided by worked examples not only failed to facilitate subsequent performance, it actually retarded learning
limits: Secondary account; no N given in the review. A boundary condition inside the founding programme.
agent_relevance: An example whose pieces are in different places (figure in one block, reasoning in another) can fail. Keep stored examples self-contained.

source: Catrambone and Holyoak (1990) and Catrambone (1994-1998), as summarised by Atkinson et al. (2000): subgoal labels in worked examples
finding: Labelling or visually grouping the subgoals inside an example improves transfer to problems that need an adapted procedure. The presence of a label mattered more than its wording. Visual separation of step groups worked as well as labels. Protocols showed labels prompt learners to explain why steps belong together.
numbers: Poisson study: 4 examples, 6 transfer items (2 similar, 4 novel). Groups equal on similar items and most novel items; highlighted group better on one novel item. Later studies repeatedly found a label advantage.
quote: it is the presence of a label, not necessarily its semantic content, that influences subgoal formation
limits: The 1990 effect was small (one item). Later effects come mostly from one lab. No N in the review.
agent_relevance: Direct support for storing the subgoal library with subgoal labels and grouped steps rather than a flat trace.

source: Reed and Bolstad (1991) Use of examples and procedures in problem solving. J Exp Psych: Learning, Memory, and Cognition 17(4), 753-766, experiment 1
finding: College students built equations for work-rate word problems from a simple example, a procedure list, or both. A three-parameter model (chance of success by matching the example m, by following a rule r, by general knowledge g) fitted the group data. Example matching is strong when the test item matches the example and falls as the number of needed transformations rises.
numbers: 65 college algebra students. Percent correct over 4 transformation levels: procedures 15%, example 34%, example plus procedures 42%. Method F(2,62)=6.01, p<.01. Fitted m=.96, r=.65, g=.45. Model explained 94% of variance.
limits: Three free parameters on 12 cells; the authors note the estimates over-predict success on some quantities. One task type.
agent_relevance: A small formal model of how an example transfers: reuse probability decays with distance from the example. Could guide which stored example to retrieve for a new item.

source: Reed and Bolstad (1991) experiment 2: simple versus complex example
finding: One example is not enough. Two examples (simple plus complex) beat every other group, including an example plus procedures. A complex example alone was no better than a simple one alone.
numbers: Six groups, percent correct over 4 transformation levels: procedures 7%, complex example 32%, simple example 38%, complex plus procedures 45%, simple plus procedures 47%, simple plus complex 65%. After rescoring: 7, 38, 38, 48, 49, 70%. Group effect F(5,168)=10.96, p<.001. Six-parameter model explained 94% of variance.
limits: With Quilici and Mayer (three examples no better than one for categorisation) this says contrast between examples matters, not count.
agent_relevance: Store at least two contrasting examples per subgoal class, not many near-copies.

source: Atkinson et al. (2000) on Paas and van Merrienboer (1994): variability of worked examples
finding: Variability across examples helps transfer only when load is kept low by using worked examples. Worked examples gave a main effect; variability gave none alone; the two interacted.
numbers: Four groups (low or high variability x practice or worked), six learning problems, six-item transfer test requiring new combinations of learned subgoals.
limits: Technical school geometry; N not given in the review.
agent_relevance: Variety among stored examples pays only when each is easy to absorb. Do not mix many problem types in one prompt for a weak model.

source: Nathan, Mertz and Ryan (1994) Learning through self-explanation of mathematics examples: effects of cognitive load. AERA paper
finding: Crossed self-explanation (SE) with load (study an example versus generate your own solution) in algebra. For story-problem translation, both SE and studying examples helped and interacted: only self-explainers who studied examples improved. For algebra manipulation (procedural) there was no significant effect.
numbers: N=32 university students, two sessions 1-2 weeks apart. Translation: SE F(1,25)=5.9, p<.025; load F(1,25)=6.76, p<.02; interaction F(1,25)=7.1, p<.02. Manipulation: no main effects; SE x load p=.1.
quote: Subjects who studied examples outperformed those generating solutions
limits: Small N, conference paper, not peer reviewed. The 1-2 week delay may have weakened the Sweller and Cooper pattern, as the authors admit.
agent_relevance: Explaining a stored example is what makes it help. Conceptually rich examples gain from explanation; bare procedures do not.

source: Chi, Bassok, Lewis, Reimann and Glaser (1989) Self-explanations, as summarised by Atkinson et al. (2000)
finding: Physics-naive students studied mechanics examples. Good learners explained the missing rationale of poorly elaborated steps, monitored understanding more accurately, looked back at examples less and more narrowly when solving. Examples usually leave steps unexplained, so the learner must supply the reason.
numbers: Four differences between successful and less successful students: more explanations including deep-structure ones; more accurate self-monitoring; less look-back; more focused look-back.
limits: Correlational split by outcome with small samples. The original PDF was a scan and could not be read; causality came later from training studies.
agent_relevance: A stored example should carry its reasons; otherwise the agent must generate them before reuse.

source: Bielaczyc, Pirolli and Brown (1995); Renkl, Stark, Gruber and Mandl (1998), as summarised by Atkinson et al. (2000): training self-explanation
finding: Explicit training in self-explanation raised explanation quality and later performance. A 15-minute training (rationale, one modelled example, one coached example) raised self-explanation by about two standard deviations and improved transfer. Low prior-knowledge learners gained most on near transfer.
numbers: Renkl et al. 1998: self-explanation effect about 2 SD; transfer improved reliably; aptitude-treatment interaction on near transfer. Bielaczyc et al. 1995: explicit beat implicit training on LISP.
limits: Review figures only; N not stated. Domains were compound interest and LISP.
agent_relevance: Asking for goal and action per step costs little for an LLM; human data say it matters most for the weakest starting point.

source: Stark (1999) incomplete examples versus Paas (1992), as summarised by Atkinson et al. (2000)
finding: Stark put blanks into Renkl's examples so learners had to anticipate the next step, then gave feedback. Incomplete examples drew more real explanation, less rereading, and better transfer than complete ones. Paas (1992) found no difference between incomplete and complete examples.
numbers: Direction only: incomplete better in Stark; no difference in Paas. No figures in the review.
limits: Reviewers say Paas did not aim to test completeness. Labs disagree.
agent_relevance: Completion format is a live design choice: blank one step and check the agent can fill it; do not expect a large gain.

source: Barbieri, Miller-Cotto, Clerjuste and Chawla (2023) A meta-analysis of the worked examples effect on mathematics performance. Educational Psychology Review 35
finding: First published meta-analysis for maths. Average effect is medium. Studies that added self-explanation prompts did worse than worked examples without prompts. Correct examples alone beat incorrect-only or mixed sets. Effect was similar for initial acquisition and for practice.
numbers: 8033 abstracts screened; 43 articles, 55 studies, 181 effect sizes. RVE average g=0.48, p=0.01 (abstract page).
quote: The worked examples effect yields a medium effect on mathematics outcomes whether used for practice or initial skill acquisition
limits: Maths only. Only the abstract page was read, not the tables. Heterogeneity was very high in the poster version.
agent_relevance: Best current size: about half a standard deviation for novices in maths. Pooled data say self-explanation prompts may not help, so test them instead of assuming.

source: Clerjuste, Chawla, Barbieri and Miller-Cotto (2022) Meta-analysis of worked examples, conference poster (interim numbers)
finding: Interim numbers: 46 experimental and 3 quasi-experimental studies; 32 articles used correct examples, 7 incorrect, 4 faded. Only 5 of 40 articles were published by 2007, when the IES practice guide rated the evidence moderate. No moderator was significant at that stage.
numbers: 185 effect sizes from -1.80 to 4.66; 41 negative, 144 positive. g=0.43, 95% CI 0.31-0.55, I-squared 94.46%.
limits: Poster, superseded by the journal version (g=0.48). Shows 41 of 185 effect sizes pointed the wrong way.
agent_relevance: About a fifth of effect sizes are negative, so the effect is not guaranteed. Test per problem class.

source: Shareghi Najar and Mitrovic (2014) Examples and tutored problems: is alternating examples and problems the best instructional strategy? Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning 9(3)
finding: In SQL-Tutor, learning from examples only (EO) was worse than problems only (PO) or alternating examples and problems (AEP). Novices learned most from AEP; advanced students learned the same from AEP and PO. The pure worked-example advantage did not replicate when problem solving had tutor feedback.
numbers: N=34 (PO 12, AEP 11, EO 11). Post-test group difference p=.02; EO below AEP p=.02 and below PO p=.09. Effect sizes on normalised gain: AEP vs PO 0.04; EO contrasts about 1.0 to 1.15. EO students spent much less time and attempted fewer tasks.
limits: Small N, single 90-minute session, university students. The PDF table layout is garbled, so only stated p values and the effect-size range are used.
agent_relevance: Our problems get code checks, which act like tutor feedback. This predicts alternating beats examples only.

source: Manson and Ayres (2019) How errors should be flagged and worked examples structured when giving feedback to novice learners of mathematics. Educational Psychology
finding: Grade 8 maths. Full worked examples used as feedback beat partial formats (single-step and completion) on learning gain. Flagging errors made no difference.
numbers: Experiment 1: 73 students started, 19 excluded, 54 analysed. Table means appear as full 4.43 (SD 2.62) versus single-step 2.46 (SD 2.80) at post-test, pre-test about 2.4 in both; column labels in the extracted text are ambiguous.
limits: Contradicts the claim that partial examples do as well as full ones; here learners were novices who had failed items. Means are approximate.
agent_relevance: For a weak or unfamiliar class, store full solutions; use partial ones only once the class is familiar.

source: Koedinger interview (2008), IES practice guide video transcript: alternating worked examples with practice
finding: Alternate one worked example with one problem. A single example can mislead (3x=9 so x=3 invites copying the coefficient); a contrasting second example exposes the wrong rule. Benefits are deeper learning and 20 to a third less time to the same level.
numbers: Time saving 'sometimes 20 percent, sometimes like a third' (spoken, no table).
quote: you can get to a better understanding in less time, sometimes 20 percent, sometimes like a third less time
limits: Interview, no data. Good for mechanism, not for size.
agent_relevance: The two-example argument maps onto the library: one stored example can be over-fitted; keep a contrasting pair.

source: Sweller, van Merrienboer and Paas (2019) Cognitive architecture and instructional design: 20 years later. Educational Psychology Review 31, worked example section
finding: Core theory: conventional problems are solved by means-ends analysis, which uses much working memory and leaves little for building schemas. Worked examples remove the search, so attention goes to states and operators. The effect was first reported by Sweller and Cooper (1985) in algebra. Later forms: product examples, process examples, modelling examples.
numbers: Theory statement, no pooled number.
quote: conventional problems ... solved by means-ends analysis, a process that is exceptionally expensive of working memory capacity
limits: Written by the theory's authors. Notes the effect is weaker for experts and good examples are hard to design.
agent_relevance: A checkable mechanism for an LLM: does search over operators crowd out step-level content in context?

source: Sweller et al. (2019) on element interactivity and the reverse worked example effect (Chen, Kalyuga and Sweller 2015-2017)
finding: The worked-example effect appears for high element interactivity material (multi-step maths problems). For low element interactivity material (learning definitions) it reversed: students who generated the answer learned more than those shown it.
numbers: Direction only, from Chen et al. 2015, 2016, 2017 as summarised.
limits: Review-level report; the Chen et al. PDF could not be fetched.
agent_relevance: Use the library for multi-step procedures, not isolated facts, where generation or retrieval is better.

source: Sweller et al. (2019) on expertise reversal and guidance fading (Kalyuga et al. 2003)
finding: As expertise rises, the worked-example advantage first shrinks, then vanishes, then reverses, because the steps become redundant. Remedy: fade examples into problems.
numbers: Direction only; no figures in this section.
limits: Called a compound effect that follows from element interactivity, so it is hard to falsify in a single study.
agent_relevance: Drop or shorten an example once the agent solves that class unaided; test the cross-over per class.

source: Sweller and Cooper (1985) The use of worked examples as a substitute for problem solving in learning algebra. Cognition and Instruction 2(1), 59-89
finding: Founding study: algebra students given worked example-problem pairs did better on later problems than students who solved all problems. Secondary accounts say study time was far lower and errors fewer, but gains held for structurally similar problems (near transfer).
numbers: Not read. A search summary says problem solvers took almost six times longer in one experiment; N and per-experiment numbers not verified.
limits: Full text paywalled. The six-times figure is an unverified secondary claim.
agent_relevance: The founding result is near transfer in algebra, a closed domain with a check, the best case for us.

source: Paas (1992) Training strategies for attaining transfer of problem-solving skill in statistics: a cognitive-load approach. J Educ Psych 84(4), 429-434
finding: Three computer-based conditions: conventional problems, worked-out problems, completion (partly worked) problems. Worked and completion beat conventional on transfer; worked was best. Hypotheses held except for training time and effort.
numbers: Abstract only: no N or scores obtained.
limits: Abstract-level. Conflicts with Manson and Ayres 2019 and Stark 1999 on whether partial equals full.
agent_relevance: Completion-style examples may match full ones; evidence is weak and conflicting.

source: Renkl and Atkinson (2003) Structuring the transition from example study to problem solving in cognitive skill acquisition. Educational Psychologist 38, 15-22
finding: Proposes backward fading: remove the last solution step first, then the last two, until the learner solves alone. Intrinsic load falls as skill rises, so problem-solving demands can rise without overload.
numbers: No numbers; theory paper.
limits: Only a search summary seen.
agent_relevance: A recipe for the library: full example, then same class with last step missing, then last two, and so on.

source: Atkinson, Renkl and Merrill (2003) Transitioning from studying examples to solving problems. J Educ Psych 95(4), 774-783
finding: Fading helped near transfer but was unreliable for far transfer. Adding prompts that ask for the underlying principle fixed far transfer. Combined effects were medium to large with no extra time.
numbers: Two experiments; medium to large effects (abstract level; values not read).
limits: Abstract-level summary; not opened.
agent_relevance: Fading plus a principle-naming prompt is the combination to try first.

source: Chandler, Kalyuga, Sweller and Tuovinen (2001) When problem solving is superior to studying worked examples. J Educ Psych 93(3), 579-588
finding: With mechanical-trade apprentices, inexperienced trainees did better and reported lower mental load with worked examples. With more experience the advantage vanished, then problem solving was better.
numbers: No figures obtained.
limits: Abstract-level only.
agent_relevance: Evidence the cross-over is real for people; for the agent it must be measured.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026-10-26) Worked-example effect: studies listed
finding: Lists boundary studies: Ward and Sweller (1990), examples sometimes no better than problem solving; Nievelstein et al. (2013), efficiency gain in legal reasoning for novice and advanced students; Schwonke et al. (2009), less learning time with examples in a Geometry Cognitive Tutor, replicated with think-aloud.
numbers: No numbers on the page.
limits: Tertiary source; the page flags a Chi et al. citation as failed verification. Needs primary papers.
agent_relevance: Points to ill-structured transfer (law) as a test for non-algorithmic domains.

source: Quilici and Mayer (1996) Role of examples in how students learn to categorize statistics word problems. J Educ Psych 88
finding: Per Wikipedia, three examples per problem type did not improve categorisation over one example.
numbers: No figures obtained.
limits: Second-hand. Contrasts with Reed and Bolstad where a second, different example helped; contrast, not count, may drive it.
agent_relevance: Do not stack many near-identical examples.

source: Nievelstein, van Gog, van Dijck and Boshuizen (2013) The worked example and expertise reversal effect in less structured tasks: learning to reason about legal cases. Contemporary Educational Psychology 38
finding: Per Wikipedia, the efficiency gain held for novice and advanced law students on a less structured task, so the effect is not limited to algorithmic domains.
numbers: No figures obtained.
limits: Second-hand. Narrows the claim that the effect works best in algorithmic domains.
agent_relevance: Examples may help on open-ended agent tasks too, but test it.

source: Zhu and Simon (1987) Learning mathematics from examples and by doing. Cognition and Instruction 4(3)
finding: Classroom study teaching factorisation from sequences of examples and problems. Atkinson et al. call it the first and possibly most cited classroom worked-examples study. Linked to a production-system model of learning from examples.
numbers: No figures obtained; PDF download failed (403).
limits: Only the review description and a search summary seen.
agent_relevance: Early computational model: examples become production rules, which is what a subgoal library does.
